items.title: Jeff Riddick Interview, 1983-07-14
items.q: When W.C. Handy played up in the courthouse... my mother, knowing how much I loved that, used to let me go.

ctx.x: So they had music in the quarter, but what kind of music was it?

It was cabaret style. Regular dance music of popular music at the time. The music that was popular at that time. For instance, Yes Sir, That's My Baby. Margie. All of those things. But the things that were already written were some 25 or 30 years the generation before that. stuff very shady, Mahogany Hall was. It's hard for me to go back further than that for the simple reason I am not a native of New Orleans. Had I been a native of New Orleans, I could tell you how it all began, so to speak. But I'm not. I'm a…
Different times. Yeah. You must have learned tunes from your daddy. Oh my lord, yes. Mississippi

items.title: Jeff Riddick Interview, 1983-07-14
items.q: And it was from Handy that I learned all of the St. Louis blues and the Memphis blues.

ctx.x: Back up to Mississippi. Were there any bands around Oakland or Jossman or Tempo?

No. No. No. Just, I'll tell you what. They used to have bands to come in. Now, for instance, I sat on W.C. Handy Handy's knee when I was a little bitty fella. And he and my father were personal friends. Handy, of course, was from Memphis. And it was from Handy that I learned all of the St. Louis blues and the Memphis blues. And I can tell you an instance. When I was playing with Sharky, someone asked for the Memphis blues. And no one in the band knew anything about the Memphis blues but the last part of it.…
Did you ever get around Tippo, Mississippi?
